definition: Banal means dull, commonplace, and lacking originality.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word banal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know banal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The critic dismissed the summer blockbuster as banal, complaining that its plot recycled the same tired rescue mission audiences had already seen a dozen times.
Something ordinary is simply common without being a flaw, while something banal is so unoriginal that it bores its audience.
A banal remark is dull and overfamiliar, but a vapid one is completely empty of thought or meaning.

Trite describes language or an idea gone stale from constant overuse: it was fresh once, and endless repetition drained the life from it. Banal is dull from the very start, commonplace and unoriginal, with no freshness to lose in the first place.

Humdrum describes the boring sameness of routine, like humdrum chores or a humdrum commute. Banal is a criticism of originality rather than of routine: a banal remark can arrive in the middle of an exciting day and still say nothing new at all.

Hackneyed describes stock phrases and plot devices that writers have leaned on for so long they have become cliches. Banal is broader and blames the thought itself: a banal idea is commonplace and unoriginal even if no one has phrased it that exact way before.

The recycled, interchangeable slogans show no originality at all, which is exactly what makes them banal.
Banal is a criticism of originality, not of craftsmanship: a banal movie can be slickly produced and still say nothing new.
It is most often applied to remarks, plots, slogans, and ideas rather than to physical objects.
